provenance.extraction: Only workflow identity, result objects and verbatim rendered-prompt excerpts; environment/provider/account/usage fields omitted. Prompt excerpts begin at the application template and end before native output-schema instructions.

dataflow: Each request passes through auth.load_logged_in_user, which reads session['user_id']; absent IDs set g.user=None, while present IDs cause a parameterized SELECT against the configured SQLite database and store the row in g.user.
login_required checks g.user and redirects anonymous callers to auth.login; authenticated callers continue to the protected view.

Registration reads request.form username/password, validates non-empty values, hashes passwords with generate_password_hash, inserts using SQL parameters, commits, flashes errors, and renders auth/register.html or redirects to auth.login.

Login reads request.form credentials, performs a parameterized username lookup, verifies the stored hash with check_password_hash, clears the session, stores the database user ID in session, and redirects to the index; failures flash an error and render auth/login.html.
blog.index executes a parameterized-free static SELECT joining post and user, orders by created descending, and passes rows to blog/index.html.
Create reads title/body from request.form, inserts them with the current authenticated user ID using SQL parameters, commits, and renders blog/create.html on GET or validation failure.

Update first calls get_post(id), which performs a parameterized post/user lookup, returns 404 for a missing post, and returns 403 when the post author_id differs from g.user['id']; valid POST data is then written with a parameterized UPDATE and rendered or redirected.
Delete likewise calls get_post(id) for existence and author authorization, then performs a parameterized DELETE and redirects to the index.

Templates inherit from base.html; base.html reads g.user, renders authentication navigation, flashed messages, and child content. Blog templates consume database rows and request.form values; edit controls are conditionally rendered when g.user['id'] equals the post author_id.
get_db creates one SQLite connection per application/request context, uses sqlite3.Row, and close_db closes it during teardown. init_db executes schema.sql; the init-db CLI command invokes it.
Tests create isolated temporary SQLite databases, initialize schema and fixture data, exercise authentication, authorization, CRUD, database teardown/CLI behavior, and factory routes.
results.map_area: Pinned Flaskr tutorial: application factory, authentication/session handling, author-only blog edits, SQLite schema, templates, and upstream tests
entrypoints: GET /hello via create_app.hello returns plain text.
GET / via blog.index queries all posts joined with their users and renders blog/index.html.
GET/POST /auth/register via auth.register validates form fields, hashes the password, inserts the user, commits, flashes validation errors, and redirects successful registration to /auth/login.
GET/POST /auth/login via auth.login queries by username, verifies the password hash, clears the session, stores session['user_id'], and redirects successful login to /.
GET /auth/logout via auth.logout clears the session and redirects to /.
GET/POST /create via blog.create is protected by login_required; it validates title, inserts a post with author_id=g.user['id'], commits, and redirects to /.
GET/POST /<int:id>/update via blog.update is protected by login_required; it loads the post with author checking, validates title, updates title/body by id, commits, and redirects to /.
POST /<int:id>/delete via blog.delete is protected by login_required; it loads the post with author checking, deletes it by id, commits, and redirects to /.
Flask app startup registers db teardown/CLI integration and auth/blog blueprints; the root endpoint aliases blog.index.
observations: The source implements authentication with hashed passwords and session-based user identification.
Author-only edit and delete enforcement is performed server-side in get_post and is also reflected in the index template's conditional edit link.
All mutation queries shown use SQL parameter binding for user input or route-derived IDs.
The index route is public; registration, login, and logout are public; create, update, and delete require an authenticated user, with update/delete additionally requiring post authorship.

The test suite explicitly covers login-required redirects, author-required 403 responses, missing-post 404 responses, CRUD effects, session loading/clearing, database teardown, and the init-db CLI command.
No defect is asserted; this record is a source-derived request, session, database, authorization, and rendering map.
trust_boundaries: HTTP request form fields enter through request.form at registration, login, create, and update endpoints; application validation checks required username, password, and title fields before writes.
The signed Flask session carries user_id between requests; auth.load_logged_in_user treats it as an identifier and resolves the corresponding user from SQLite.
Database records are trusted as application state after parameterized queries; author authorization compares the stored post author_id with the authenticated g.user id before update/delete.
Password input crosses into password-hashing and verification functions; stored passwords are hashes rather than plaintext values.
Template rendering receives database rows, g.user, request.form, and flashed messages. Jinja template interpolation is used for displayed values and form values.
SQLite is addressed through app.config['DATABASE']; schema.sql defines user/post tables, uniqueness for usernames, required fields, and the post-to-user foreign key.
Tests cross the application boundary through Flask's test client and cross the database boundary through temporary SQLite files and fixture SQL.

evidence: flaskr/auth.py:53-81 reads request.form username/password, validates non-empty values, hashes passwords, executes INSERT with (?, ?), commits, flashes errors, and renders or redirects.
flaskr/auth.py:87-109 performs SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = ?; verifies the stored hash, clears the session, stores session["user_id"], and renders login errors.
flaskr/auth.py:32-43 reads session.get("user_id") and resolves it with SELECT * FROM user WHERE id = ? into g.user; flaskr/auth.py:19-29 redirects anonymous users.
flaskr/blog.py:20-25 performs a static SELECT for the public index; flaskr/blog.py:40-57 binds the route ID with WHERE p.id = ? and enforces author_id == g.user["id"].
flaskr/blog.py:64-83 validates and inserts title, body, and g.user["id"] with bound parameters; flaskr/blog.py:92-110 validates and updates title/body/id with bound parameters.
flaskr/blog.py:121-125 authorizes through get_post before executing DELETE FROM post WHERE id = ? with a bound ID.
flaskr/db.py:14-20 creates one configured SQLite connection per app context and sets sqlite3.Row; flaskr/db.py:23-30 closes it during teardown.
flaskr/schema.sql:7-20 defines unique non-null usernames, non-null password/title/body fields, and the author_id foreign key.

flaskr/templates/base.html:7-23 renders g.user navigation and flashed messages; flaskr/templates/blog/index.html:15-22 renders title, username, body, and conditionally renders the edit link when the current user is the author.
flaskr/templates/blog/create.html:8-13 and flaskr/templates/blog/update.html:8-18 render request.form/database values using Jinja interpolation and provide create/update/delete forms.

tests/test_auth.py:32-69 covers registration validation, login success/failure, session user loading, and logout clearing; tests/test_blog.py:19-44 covers login-required, author-required, and missing-post behavior; tests/test_blog.py:46-82 covers CRUD and title validation.

No actual source defect was established by these checks; parameter binding, server-side author checks, password hashing, and Jinja rendering assumptions are consistent with the reviewed tests and application flow.

results.summary: Default predictable Flask secret key enables session forgery when configuration is not overridden.
results.explanation: The application hard-codes SECRET_KEY="dev" as its default. If deployed without overriding this setting, an attacker who knows the tutorial default can forge Flask session cookies, set a chosen user_id, and access or act through authenticated routes as that user.
trigger_flow: Attacker signs a crafted session cookie using the public default key.
Flask accepts the cookie and load_logged_in_user resolves the attacker-selected user_id.
login_required permits access to create, update, or delete routes.
Author checks may then authorize actions as the forged user.
results.malicious_input_example: A forged Flask session cookie signed with the known key "dev" containing {"user_id":1}.

results.summary: Authenticated state-changing routes lack CSRF protection.
results.explanation: The state-changing registration, login, create, update, and delete forms have no CSRF token validation. A malicious site can submit cross-origin POST requests from a victim's browser while the victim's Flask session cookie is included, potentially creating content or modifying/deleting the victim's posts.
trigger_flow: Victim logs in and retains the Flask session cookie.
Attacker lures the victim to a malicious origin.
The malicious origin submits a cross-site POST to /<id>/delete or /<id>/update.
The browser sends the victim's session cookie; login_required and author checks accept the request, causing the state change.
results.malicious_actor: Unauthenticated remote attacker controlling a malicious website
results.malicious_input_example: A malicious page auto-submitting <form action="https://target.example/1/delete" method="post"></form> while the victim is logged in.

dataflow: Each request passes through auth.load_logged_in_user, which reads session['user_id']; absent IDs set g.user=None, while present IDs cause a parameterized SELECT against the configured SQLite database and store the row in g.user.
login_required checks g.user and redirects anonymous callers to auth.login; authenticated callers continue to the protected view.

Registration reads request.form username/password, validates non-empty values, hashes passwords with generate_password_hash, inserts using SQL parameters, commits, flashes errors, and renders auth/register.html or redirects to auth.login.

Login reads request.form credentials, performs a parameterized username lookup, verifies the stored hash with check_password_hash, clears the session, stores the database user ID in session, and redirects to the index; failures flash an error and render auth/login.html.
blog.index executes a parameterized-free static SELECT joining post and user, orders by created descending, and passes rows to blog/index.html.
Create reads title/body from request.form, inserts them with the current authenticated user ID using SQL parameters, commits, and renders blog/create.html on GET or validation failure.

Update first calls get_post(id), which performs a parameterized post/user lookup, returns 404 for a missing post, and returns 403 when the post author_id differs from g.user['id']; valid POST data is then written with a parameterized UPDATE and rendered or redirected.
Delete likewise calls get_post(id) for existence and author authorization, then performs a parameterized DELETE and redirects to the index.

Templates inherit from base.html; base.html reads g.user, renders authentication navigation, flashed messages, and child content. Blog templates consume database rows and request.form values; edit controls are conditionally rendered when g.user['id'] equals the post author_id.
get_db creates one SQLite connection per application/request context, uses sqlite3.Row, and close_db closes it during teardown. init_db executes schema.sql; the init-db CLI command invokes it.
Tests create isolated temporary SQLite databases, initialize schema and fixture data, exercise authentication, authorization, CRUD, database teardown/CLI behavior, and factory routes.

GET/POST /<int:id>/update via blog.update is protected by login_required; it loads the post with author checking, validates title, updates title/body by id, commits, and redirects to /.
POST /<int:id>/delete via blog.delete is protected by login_required; it loads the post with author checking, deletes it by id, commits, and redirects to /.

observations: The source implements authentication with hashed passwords and session-based user identification.

trust_boundaries: HTTP request form fields enter through request.form at registration, login, create, and update endpoints; application validation checks required username, password, and title fields before writes.
The signed Flask session carries user_id between requests; auth.load_logged_in_user treats it as an identifier and resolves the corresponding user from SQLite.
Database records are trusted as application state after parameterized queries; author authorization compares the stored post author_id with the authenticated g.user id before update/delete.
Password input crosses into password-hashing and verification functions; stored passwords are hashes rather than plaintext values.
Template rendering receives database rows, g.user, request.form, and flashed messages. Jinja template interpolation is used for displayed values and form values.
